{{Short description|Common point(s) shared by two lines in Euclidean geometry}}
[[Image:Line-Line Intersection.png|400px|thumb|right|Two intersecting lines]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''intersection of a line and a line''' can be the [[empty set]], a single [[point (geometry)|point]], or a [[Line (geometry)|line]] (if they coincide). Distinguishing these cases and finding the [[Intersection (Euclidean geometry)|intersection]] have uses, for example, in [[computer graphics]], [[motion planning]], and [[collision detection]].

In a [[Euclidean space]], if two lines are not [[coplanarity |coplanar]], they have no point of intersection <ref>{{Cite web |first=Jeremy |last=Cook |date=November 21, 2023 |title=Coplanar Lines in Geometry {{!}} Definition, Diagrams & Examples |url=https://study.com/academy/lesson/coplanar-lines-in-geometry-definition-lesson-quiz.html#:~:text=Non%2Dcoplanar%20lines%20are%20lines%20that%20are%20not%20on%20the,not%20in%20the%20same%20plane. |access-date=November 1, 2024}}</ref> and are called [[skew lines]]. If they are coplanar, however, there are three possibilities: if they coincide (are the same line), they have all of their [[infinity|infinitely many]] points in common; if they are distinct but have the same direction, they are said to be [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] and have no points in common; otherwise, they have a single point of intersection, denoted as [[singleton set]], for instance <math>\{A\}</math>.

[[Non-Euclidean geometry]] describes spaces in which one line may not be parallel to any other lines, such as a sphere, and spaces where multiple lines through a single point may all be parallel to another line.{{Further explanation needed|reason=This is an encyclopedic topic, go write about it|date=June 2022}} In [[Spherical geometry|spherical]] and [[Elliptic geometry|elliptic]] geometries, every pair of lines intersects, while in [[Hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic]] geometry there exist infinitely many distinct lines through a given point that do not intersect a given line.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Anderson |first=J. W. |title=Hyperbolic Geometry |publisher=Springer |year=2005 |isbn= |edition=2nd}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> Projective geometry provides a unifying framework in which these different behaviors can be described by extending the notion of intersection to include ideal points, so that any two distinct lines intersect in exactly one point.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vajda |first=S. |last2=Hughes |first2=D. R. |last3=Piper |first3=F. C. |date=1974 |title=Projective Planes. |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/2344563 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General) |volume=137 |issue=2 |pages=269 |doi=10.2307/2344563 |issn=0035-9238|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Formulas ==
{{see also|Skew lines#Formulas}}

A [[necessary condition]] for two lines to intersect is that they are in the same plane&mdash;that is, are not skew lines. Satisfaction of this condition is equivalent to the [[tetrahedron]] with vertices at two of the points on one line and two of the points on the other line being [[degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerate]] in the sense of having zero [[volume]]. For the algebraic form of this condition, see {{slink|Skew lines|Testing for skewness}}.

===Given two points on each line===

First we consider the intersection of two lines {{math|''L''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''L''<sub>2</sub>}} in two-dimensional space, with line {{math|''L''<sub>1</sub>}} being defined by two distinct points {{math|(''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|(''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>)}}, and line {{math|''L''<sub>2</sub>}} being defined by two distinct points {{math|(''x''<sub>3</sub>, ''y''<sub>3</sub>)}} and {{math|(''x''<sub>4</sub>, ''y''<sub>4</sub>)}}.<ref name="Wolfram">{{MathWorld|title=Line-Line Intersection|id=Line-LineIntersection|access-date=2008-01-10}}</ref>

The intersection {{mvar|P}} of line {{math|''L''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''L''<sub>2</sub>}} can be defined using [[determinant]]s.

:<math>
P_x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1\\x_2 & y_2\end{vmatrix} &  \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & 1\\x_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\\\ \begin{vmatrix} x_3 & y_3\\x_4 & y_4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix} x_3 & 1\\x_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} \end{vmatrix} }
{\begin{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & 1\\x_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} &  \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & 1\\y_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\\\ \begin{vmatrix} x_3 & 1\\x_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix} y_3 & 1\\y_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} \end{vmatrix}}\,\!
\qquad
P_y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1\\x_2 & y_2\end{vmatrix} &  \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & 1\\y_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\\\ \begin{vmatrix} x_3 & y_3\\x_4 & y_4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix} y_3 & 1\\y_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} \end{vmatrix} }
{\begin{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & 1\\x_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} &  \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & 1\\y_2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\\\ \begin{vmatrix} x_3 & 1\\x_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix} y_3 & 1\\y_4 & 1\end{vmatrix} \end{vmatrix}}\,\!
</math>

The determinants can be written out as:

: <math>
\begin{align}
P_x&= \frac{(x_1 y_2-y_1 x_2)(x_3-x_4)-(x_1-x_2)(x_3 y_4-y_3 x_4)}{(x_1-x_2) (y_3-y_4) - (y_1-y_2) (x_3-x_4)}
\\[4px]
P_y&= \frac{(x_1 y_2-y_1 x_2)(y_3-y_4)-(y_1-y_2)(x_3 y_4-y_3 x_4)}{(x_1-x_2) (y_3-y_4) - (y_1-y_2) (x_3-x_4)}
\end{align}
</math>

When the two lines are parallel or coincident, the denominator is zero.

===Given two points on each line segment===
{{see also|Intersection (geometry)#Two line segments}}

The intersection point above is for the infinitely long lines defined by the points, rather than the [[line segment]]s between the points, and can produce an intersection point not contained in either of the two line segments. In order to find the position of the intersection with respect to the line segments, we can define lines {{math|''L''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''L''<sub>2</sub>}} in terms of first degree [[Bézier curve#Linear curves|Bézier]] parameters:

: <math>
L_1 =   \begin{bmatrix}x_1     \\ y_1\end{bmatrix}
    + t \begin{bmatrix}x_2-x_1 \\ y_2-y_1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
L_2 =   \begin{bmatrix}x_3     \\ y_3\end{bmatrix}
    + u \begin{bmatrix}x_4-x_3 \\ y_4-y_3\end{bmatrix}
</math>

(where {{mvar|t}} and {{mvar|u}} are real numbers). The intersection point of the lines is found with one of the following values of {{mvar|t}} or {{mvar|u}}, where

: <math>
t = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_3 & x_3-x_4\\y_1-y_3 & y_3-y_4\end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_2 & x_3-x_4\\y_1-y_2 & y_3-y_4\end{vmatrix}} = \frac{(x_1 - x_3)(y_3-y_4)-(y_1-y_3)(x_3-x_4)}{(x_1-x_2)(y_3-y_4)-(y_1-y_2)(x_3-x_4)}
</math>
and 
: <math>
u = - \frac{\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_2 & x_1-x_3\\y_1-y_2 & y_1-y_3\end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_2 & x_3-x_4\\y_1-y_2 & y_3-y_4\end{vmatrix}} = -\frac{(x_1 - x_2)(y_1-y_3)-(y_1-y_2)(x_1-x_3)}{(x_1-x_2)(y_3-y_4)-(y_1-y_2)(x_3-x_4)},
</math>
with
: <math>
(P_x, P_y)= \bigl(x_1 + t (x_2-x_1),\; y_1 + t (y_2-y_1)\bigr) \quad \text{or} \quad (P_x, P_y) = \bigl(x_3 + u (x_4-x_3),\; y_3 + u (y_4-y_3)\bigr)
</math>

There will be an intersection if {{math|0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ 1}} and {{math|0 ≤ ''u'' ≤ 1}}. The intersection point falls within the first line segment if {{math|0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ 1}}, and it falls within the second line segment if {{math|0 ≤ ''u'' ≤ 1}}. These inequalities can be tested without the need for division, allowing rapid determination of the existence of any line segment intersection before calculating its exact point.<ref name="GGIII">{{cite book |last1=Antonio |first1=Franklin |editor-last=Kirk |editor-first=David |title=Graphics Gems III |publisher=Academic Press, Inc. |date=1992 |pages=199–202 |chapter=Chapter IV.6: Faster Line Segment Intersection |isbn=0-12-059756-X}}</ref>

In the case where the two line segments share an x axis and <math> x_2 = x_1 + 1 </math>, <math> t </math> and <math> u </math> simplify to
<math display=block>
t = u = \frac{y_1 - y_3}{y_1 - y_2 - y_3 + y_4}, 
</math>
with
<math display=block>
(P_x, P_y)= \bigl(x_1 + t,\; y_1 + t (y_2-y_1)\bigr) \quad \text{or} \quad (P_x, P_y) = \bigl(x_1 + t,\; y_3 + t (y_4-y_3)\bigr).
</math>

===Given two line equations===
{{see also|Intersection (geometry)#Two lines}}

The {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} coordinates of the point of intersection of two non-vertical lines can easily be found using the following substitutions and rearrangements.

Suppose that two lines have the equations {{math|''y'' {{=}} ''ax'' + ''c''}} and {{math|''y'' {{=}} ''bx'' + ''d''}} where {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}} are the [[slope]]s (gradients) of the lines and where {{mvar|c}} and {{mvar|d}} are the {{mvar|y}}-intercepts of the lines. At the point where the two lines intersect (if they do), both {{mvar|y}} coordinates will be the same, hence the following equality:

:<math>ax+c = bx+d.</math>

We can rearrange this expression in order to extract the value of {{mvar|x}},

:<math>ax-bx = d-c,</math>
and so, 
:<math>x = \frac{d-c}{a-b}.</math>

To find the {{mvar|y}} coordinate, all we need to do is substitute the value of {{mvar|x}} into either one of the two line equations, for example, into the first:

:<math>y = a\frac{d-c}{a-b}+c.</math>

Hence, the point of intersection is 
:<math>P = \left( \frac{d-c}{a-b}, a\frac{d-c}{a-b}+c \right) .</math>
Note that if {{math|''a'' {{=}} ''b''}} then the two lines are [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] and they do not intersect, unless {{math|''c'' {{=}} ''d''}} as well, in which case the lines are coincident and they intersect at every point.

=== Using homogeneous coordinates  ===

By using [[homogeneous coordinates]], the intersection point of two implicitly defined lines can be determined quite easily. In 2D, every point can be defined as a projection of a 3D point, given as the ordered triple {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''w'')}}. The mapping from 3D to 2D coordinates is {{math|(''x''′, ''y''′) {{=}} ({{sfrac|''x''|''w''}}, {{sfrac|''y''|''w''}})}}. We can convert 2D points to homogeneous coordinates by defining them as {{math|(''x'', ''y'', 1)}}.

Assume that we want to find intersection of two infinite lines in 2-dimensional space, defined as {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>''x'' + ''b''<sub>1</sub>''y'' + ''c''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 0}} and {{math|''a''<sub>2</sub>''x'' + ''b''<sub>2</sub>''y'' + ''c''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} 0}}. We can represent these two lines in [[line coordinates]] as  {{math|''U''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} (''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''c''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|''U''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} (''a''<sub>2</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, ''c''<sub>2</sub>)}}. The intersection {{math|''P''′}} of two lines is then simply given by<ref>{{Cite web |last=Birchfield |first=Stanley |date=1998-04-23 |title=Homogeneous coordinates |url=http://robotics.stanford.edu/~birch/projective/node4.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000929025956/http://robotics.stanford.edu/~birch/projective/node4.html |archive-date=2000-09-29 |website=robotics.stanford.edu |accessdate=2015-08-18}}</ref>

:<math>P' = (a_p, b_p, c_p) = U_1 \times U_2 = (b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1, a_2 c_1-a_1 c_2, a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)</math>

If {{math|''c<sub>p</sub>'' {{=}} 0}}, the lines do not intersect.

== More than two lines ==
{{see also|Skew lines#More than two lines}}

The intersection of two lines can be generalized to involve additional lines. The existence of and expression for the {{mvar|n}}-line intersection problem are as follows.

=== In two dimensions ===

In two dimensions, more than two lines [[almost certainly]] do not intersect at a single point. To determine if they do and, if so, to find the intersection point, write the {{mvar|i}}th equation ({{math|''i'' {{=}} 1, …, ''n''}}) as

:<math>\begin{bmatrix} a_{i1} & a_{i2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = b_i,</math>

and stack these equations into matrix form as

:<math>\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{b},</math>

where the {{mvar|i}}th row of the {{math|''n'' × 2}} matrix {{math|'''A'''}} is {{math|[''a''<sub>''i''1</sub>, ''a''<sub>''i''2</sub>]}}, {{math|'''w'''}} is the 2 × 1 vector {{math|<big><big>[</big></big>{{su|p=''x''|b=''y''}}<big><big>]</big></big>}}, and the {{mvar|i}}th element of the column vector {{math|'''b'''}} is {{math|''b''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. If {{math|'''A'''}} has independent columns, its [[matrix rank|rank]] is 2.  Then [[if and only if]] the rank of the [[augmented matrix]] {{math|['''A''' {{!}} '''b''']}} is also 2, there exists a solution of the matrix equation and thus an intersection point of the {{mvar|n}} lines. The intersection point, if it exists, is given by

:<math>\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{A}^\mathrm{g} \mathbf{b} = \left(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{A}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{b},</math>

where {{math|'''A'''<sup>g</sup>}} is the [[Moore–Penrose inverse|Moore–Penrose generalized inverse]] of {{math|'''A'''}} (which has the form shown because {{math|'''A'''}} has full column rank). Alternatively, the solution can be found by jointly solving any two independent equations. But if the rank of {{math|'''A'''}} is only 1, then if the rank of the augmented matrix is 2 there is no solution but if its rank is 1 then all of the lines coincide with each other.

=== In three dimensions ===

The above approach can be readily extended to three dimensions. In three or more dimensions, even two lines almost certainly do not intersect; pairs of non-parallel lines that do not intersect are called [[skew lines]].  But if an intersection does exist it can be found, as follows.

In three dimensions a line is represented by the intersection of two planes, each of which has an equation of the form

:<math>\begin{bmatrix} a_{i1} & a_{i2} & a_{i3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} = b_i.</math>

Thus a set of {{mvar|n}} lines can be represented by {{math|2''n''}} equations in the 3-dimensional [[coordinate vector]] {{math|'''w'''}}:

:<math>\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{b}</math>

where now {{math|'''A'''}} is {{math|2''n'' × 3}} and {{math|'''b'''}} is {{math|2''n'' × 1}}. As before there is a unique intersection point if and only if {{math|'''A'''}} has full column rank and the augmented matrix {{math|['''A''' {{!}} '''b''']}} does not, and the unique intersection if it exists is given by

:<math>\mathbf{w} = \left(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{A} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{b}.</math>

==Nearest points to skew lines==
[[File:skew_lines_shortest_distance.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|PQ, the shortest distance between two skew lines AB and CD is perpendicular to both AB and CD]]
{{main|Skew lines#Nearest points}}

In two or more dimensions, we can usually find a point that is mutually closest to two or more lines in a [[least-squares]] sense.

===In two dimensions===

In the two-dimensional case, first, represent line {{mvar|i}} as a point {{math|'''p'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} on the line and a [[unit vector|unit]] [[normal vector]] {{math|'''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, perpendicular to that line. That is, if {{math|'''x'''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|'''x'''<sub>2</sub>}} are points on line 1, then let {{math|'''p'''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} '''x'''<sub>1</sub>}} and let

:<math>\mathbf{\hat n}_1:= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \frac{\mathbf{x}_2 - \mathbf{x}_1} {\|\mathbf{x}_2-\mathbf{x}_1\|}</math>

which is the unit vector along the line, rotated by a right angle.

The distance from a point {{math|'''x'''}} to the line {{math|('''p''', '''n̂''')}} is given by

:<math>d\bigl(\mathbf{x},(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{\hat n})\bigr) = \bigl|(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{\hat n}\bigr| = \left|(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}\right| = \left|\mathbf{\hat n} ^\mathsf{T} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})\right| = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n} \mathbf{\hat n}^\mathsf{T} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})}.</math>

And so the squared distance from a point {{math|'''x'''}} to a line is

:<math>d\bigl(\mathbf{x},(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{\hat n})\bigr)^2 = (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})^\mathsf{T} \left(\mathbf{\hat n} \mathbf{\hat n}^\mathsf{T} \right) (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}).</math>

The sum of squared distances to many lines is the [[Loss function|cost function]]:

:<math>E(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}_i)^\mathsf{T} \left(\mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}\right) (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}_i).</math>

This can be rearranged:

:<math>
\begin{align}
E(\mathbf{x}) & = \sum_i \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{p}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i \\
& = \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T} \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}\right) \mathbf{x} - 2 \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T} \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i\right) + \sum_i \mathbf{p}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i.
\end{align}
</math>

To find the minimum, we differentiate with respect to {{math|'''x'''}} and set the result equal to the zero vector:

:<math>\frac{\partial E(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \boldsymbol{0} = 2 \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}\right) \mathbf{x} - 2 \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i\right) </math>

so

:<math>\left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}\right) \mathbf{x} = \sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i</math>

and so

:<math>\mathbf{x} = \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}\right)^{-1} \left(\sum_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{p}_i\right).</math>

===In more than two dimensions===

While {{math|'''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is not well-defined in more than two dimensions, this can be generalized to any number of dimensions by noting that {{math|'''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub> '''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub><sup>T</sup>}} is simply the [[symmetric matrix]] with all [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] unity except for a zero eigenvalue in the direction along the line providing a [[seminorm]] on the distance between {{math|'''p'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} and another point giving the distance to the line. In any number of dimensions, if {{math|'''v̂'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is a unit vector ''along'' the {{mvar|i}}th line, then

: <math>\mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T}</math> becomes <math>\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{\hat v}_i \mathbf{\hat v}_i^\mathsf{T}</math>

where {{math|'''I'''}} is the [[identity matrix]], and so<ref>{{cite web |last1=Traa |first1=Johannes |date=2013 |title=Least-Squares Intersection of Lines |url=http://cal.cs.illinois.edu/~johannes/research/LS_line_intersect.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170912055605/http://cal.cs.illinois.edu/~johannes/research/LS_line_intersect.pdf |archive-date=2017-09-12 |website=cal.cs.illinois.edu |accessdate=2018-08-30}}</ref>

: <math> x= \left(\sum_i \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{\hat v}_i \mathbf{\hat v}_i^\mathsf{T}\right)^{-1} \left(\sum_i \left(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{\hat v}_i \mathbf{\hat v}_i^\mathsf{T} \right) \mathbf{p}_i\right).</math>

===General derivation===
In order to find the intersection point of a set of lines, we calculate the point with minimum distance to them. Each line is defined by an origin {{math|'''a'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} and a unit direction vector {{math|'''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. The square of the distance from a point {{math|'''p'''}} to one of the lines is given from Pythagoras:

: <math> d_i^2 = \left\| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right\|^2 - \left( \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \right)^2
= \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T} \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right) - \left( \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \right)^2</math>
where {{math|('''p''' − '''a'''<sub>''i''</sub>)<sup>T</sup> '''n̂'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is the projection of {{math|'''p''' − '''a'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} on line {{mvar|i}}. The sum of distances to the square to all lines is

: <math> \sum_i d_i^2 = \sum_i \left( {\left( \mathbf{p}- \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T}} \left( \mathbf{p}- \mathbf{a}_i \right)- {\left( \left( \mathbf{p}- \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i \right)^2} \right) </math>

To minimize this expression, we differentiate it with respect to {{math|'''p'''}}.

: <math> \sum_i \left( 2\left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)- 2 \left(\left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{\hat n}_i\right) \mathbf{\hat n}_i\right)=\boldsymbol{0}
</math>

: <math> \sum_i \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right) = \sum_i \left( \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \right) \left( \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}_i \right)
</math>

which results in

: <math> \left(\sum_i\left(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \right)\right) \mathbf{p}
= \sum_i \left(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{\hat n}_i \mathbf{\hat n}_i^\mathsf{T} \right) \mathbf{a}_i</math>

where {{math|'''I'''}} is the [[identity matrix]]. This is a matrix {{math|'''Sp''' {{=}} '''C'''}}, with solution {{math|'''p''' {{=}} '''S'''<sup>+</sup>'''C'''}}, where {{math|'''S'''<sup>+</sup>}} is the [[pseudo-inverse]] of {{math|'''S'''}}.

== Non-Euclidean geometry ==
{{See also|Parallel postulate}}{{Expand section|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Euclidian and non euclidian geometry.png|alt=From left to right: Euclidean geometry, spherical geometry, and hyperbolic geometry|thumb|From left to right: Euclidean geometry, spherical geometry, and hyperbolic geometry]]
In [[spherical geometry]], lines are represented by great circles,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Exploring Hyperbolic Space |url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~kpmann/Hyperbolic%20and%20Spherical%20geometries.pdf |access-date=2022-06-03 |website=math.berkeley.edu}}</ref> defined as the intersections of a sphere <math>S^2=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x\| = R\}</math> with planes through the origin.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Coxeter |first=H. |url=https://doi.org/10.5948/9781614445166 |title=Non-Euclidean Geometry |date=1998 |publisher=American Mathematical                     Society |isbn=978-1-61444-516-6 |series=Spectrum |location=Providence, Rhode                     Island}}</ref>
[[File:Intersection of two great circles on a sphere.png|left|thumb|Intersection of two great circles on a sphere]]
Two [[Great circle|great circles]] lying in planes with unit normal vectors <math>\mathbf{\hat n}_1</math> and <math>\mathbf{\hat n}_2</math> intersect at two [[Antipodal point|antipodal points]], which (up to normalization) can be expressed by<ref>{{Cite book |last=do Carmo |first=M. P. |author-link=Manfredo do Carmo |title=Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=1976 |isbn= |pages=150-160}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=O’Neill |first=B. |title=Elementary Differential Geometry |publisher=Academic Press |year=2006 |isbn=9780120887354 |edition=2nd |pages=140-145}}</ref>

<math>\mathbf{x}= \pm\frac{\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2} {\|\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2\|}</math>

Every pair of lines intersects in two antipodal points, so there are no parallel lines in spherical geometry.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Todhunter |first=I. |title=Spherical Trigonometry: For the Use of Colleges and Schools |publisher=Macmillan |year=1893 |edition=3rd |pages=16-25}}</ref>

In [[elliptic geometry]], the space may be regarded as a quotient of spherical geometry in which antipodal points are identified. Lines in this geometry correspond to great circles with antipodal points considered equivalent, so each pair of lines intersects in exactly one point.<ref name=":1" /> Unlike spherical geometry, this identification eliminates the distinction between the two intersection points, producing a finite but unbounded space without parallel lines.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Coxeter |first=H.S.M. |author-link=H. S. M. Coxeter |title=Projective Geometry |publisher=Springer |year=2003 |edition=2nd |pages=}}</ref>

In [[hyperbolic geometry]], line–line intersection behavior differs from that of Euclidean and positively curved geometries.<ref name=":1" /> Given a line <math>\ell</math> and a point <math>P\not\in\ell</math>, there exist infinitely many distinct lines through <math>P</math> that do not intersect <math>\ell</math>.<ref name=":0" /> Two lines may intersect in exactly one point, be asymptotically parallel, or be ultraparallel (disjoint with a common perpendicular). This behavior reflects the constant negative [[Gaussian curvature]] <math>K<0</math> of [[hyperbolic space]] and the failure of the Euclidean parallel postulate. Line–line intersection is therefore not guaranteed and depends on the [[Incidence geometry|incidence]] relations of the geometry rather than on metric distance alone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Anderson |first=James W. |date=1999 |title=Hyperbolic Geometry |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-3987-4 |journal=Springer Undergraduate Mathematics Series |doi=10.1007/978-1-4471-3987-4 |issn=1615-2085|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>'''B. O’Neill''', ''Semi-Riemannian Geometry'', §4</ref>

In [[projective geometry]], any two distinct lines intersect in exactly one point by construction. This is achieved by adjoining [[Ideal point|ideal points]] (points at infinity), so that parallel lines in Euclidean geometry meet at a single projective point.<ref name=":2" /> Lines are modeled as one-dimensional projective subspaces, and incidence relations are fundamental, while notions of distance, angle, and curvature are not. Projective geometry thus provides a unifying framework in which Euclidean, elliptic, and hyperbolic geometries can be studied via appropriate projective models.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hughes, D. R. |first=Piper, F. C. |title=Projective Planes |publisher=Springer |year= |isbn= |edition=2nd}}</ref>
